ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Non-Asymptotic Bounds for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: Develop non-asymptotic sample-complexity guarantees for KernelSHAP, the most widely used randomized estimator for computing Shapley values, by analyzing its statistical properties and providing a theoretical framework for understanding its performance. Specifically, derive a bound on the mean squared error (MSE) of KernelSHAP's output in terms of the number of subsampled rows, the variance of the sampling distribution, and the condition number of the regression problem.
CONTROLS: Analyze existing implementations of KernelSHAP, identify limitations, and compare our bounds with existing results for unbiased KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: We expect to provide the first non-asymptotic guarantees for KernelSHAP, and derived technical bounds could have a large impact on understanding the relative performance of Shapley value estimators. However, the assumptions required to establish the bounds might overly simplify the real-world scenarios, making it difficult to apply our results in practice.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experiments on KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP on Real-World Datasets
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP on a range of real-world datasets from different domains, including but not limited to image classification (e.g., CIFAR-10), natural language processing (e.g., IMDB sentiment analysis), and tabular data (e.g., Bank Marketing campaign). Evaluate their accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency.
CONTROLS: Use the same implementation of KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP as in the original paper, and consider additional baselines such as SHAP and DeepLIFT. Perform a thorough hyperparameter tuning for each method to ensure a fair comparison.
COST: 32400
PREDICTION: We expect to find that LeverageSHAP outperforms KernelSHAP in terms of accuracy and robustness, especially in high-dimensional datasets. However, the performance gap might be small, and we may not observe significant differences in computational efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Sampling Distribution on Shapley Value Estimators
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of different sampling distributions on the performance of Shapley value estimators, including KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP, and unbiased KernelSHAP. Design and evaluate various sampling distributions, such as uniform, kernel-weighted, and leverage-score based, to understand their impact on the estimators' accuracy and robustness.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the estimators under different sampling distributions using the same experimental setup as in proposal 2. Useontechniques such as sensitivity analysis and robustness testing to understand the impact of the sampling distribution on the estimators.
COST: 48600
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the kernel-weighted sampling distribution used in KernelSHAP is not the optimal choice, and that other sampling distributions, such as the leverage-score based distribution, can lead to better performance. However, the best sampling distribution might depend on the specific dataset and model, making it challenging to identify a single optimal choice.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Sampling Distribution on Shapley Value Estimators
PROPOSAL: (Revised) Investigate the optimal sampling distribution for Shapley value estimators using optimization techniques. Formulate the optimization problem as maximizing the expected accuracy or minimizing the expected mean squared error (MSE) of the estimator under a given sampling distribution. Use techniques such as Bayesian optimization and gradient-based optimization to search for the optimal sampling distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare the optimal sampling distribution found using optimization with the existing kernel-weighted sampling distribution used in KernelSHAP. Evaluate the performance of the estimator using the optimal sampling distribution on a range of real-world datasets.
COST: 64800
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the optimal sampling distribution is dataset-dependent and can significantly outperform the kernel-weighted sampling distribution used in KernelSHAP. However, the optimization process might be computationally expensive, and the optimal sampling distribution might not be easy to interpret or implement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: High-Dimensional Approximations for Shapley Value Estimators
PROPOSAL: Develop efficient high-dimensional approximations for Shapley value estimators, such as KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, to enable their use on large-scale datasets. Investigate the use of sparse approximation techniques, such as sketching and compressive sensing, to reduce the computational complexity of the estimators.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed high-dimensional approximations on a range of real-world datasets. Compare the performance of the approximations with the exact estimator on smaller-scale datasets.
COST: 97200
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the proposed high-dimensional approximations can significantly reduce the computational complexity of Shapley value estimators while preserving their accuracy. However, the choice of approximation technique might depend on the specific dataset and estimator, making it challenging to identify a single optimal approach.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: High-Dimensional Approximations for Shapley Value Estimators
PROPOSAL: (Revised) Develop and evaluate a scalable implementation of LeveragingSHAP that leverages iterative low-rank approximation techniques, such as the Alternating Least Squares (ALS) algorithm, to efficiently compute the Shapley values in high-dimensional spaces. Compare the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed implementation with existing high-dimensional approximations and exact implementations.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the proposed implementation on a range of real-world datasets with varying numbers of features and instances. Compare the results with existing estimators, including KernelSHAP and unbiased KernelSHAP.
COST: 129600
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the proposed implementation of LeveragingSHAP with ALS can efficiently compute Shapley values in high-dimensional spaces while preserving their accuracy. However, the convergence of the ALS algorithm might be sensitive to the choice of initialization and other hyperparameters, making it challenging to achieve consistent results across different datasets.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the development of provably efficient algorithms for estimating Shapley values, with a focus on high-dimensional spaces. Explore the use of optimization techniques, such as stochastic gradient descent and alternating minimization, to efficiently compute the Shapley values while ensuring their accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed algorithms with existing high-dimensional approximations and exact implementations. Evaluate the theoretical guarantees and empirical performance of the proposed algorithms on a range of real-world datasets.

PREDICTION: We expect to find that the proposed algorithms can efficiently compute Shapley values in high-dimensional spaces while preserving their accuracy. However, the theoretical guarantees might require strong assumptions on the data distribution, making it challenging to achieve consistent results across different datasets.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the performance of Shapley value estimators in sensitive domains, such as healthcare and finance, where predicting certain outcomes can have significant consequences. Evaluate the accuracy and fairness of different Shapley value estimators, such as KernelSHAP and LeverageSHAP, on real-world datasets from these domains.

However, the results might be sensitive to the choice of estimator and its hyperparameters, and the fairness of the estimators might be challenging to guarantee in practice.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of Shapley value estimation for large-scale deep learning models, particularly those with millions of parameters. Develop a scalable and efficient algorithm for computing Shapley values for deep learning models, and evaluate its performance on a range of benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed algorithm with existing Shapley value estimation methods on deep learning models. Evaluate the scalability and efficiency of the algorithm using metrics such as runtime and memory usage.

However, the scalability of the algorithm might be challenged by the increasing complexity of deep learning models, and the results might require further optimization for practical applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Long-term Temporal Dependencies in Satellite Image Time Series forecasting via Multimodal Transformers
PROPOSAL: We experiment with adapting the hybrid transformer architecture of ViLBERT to multimodal satellite image sequences, injecting temporal information via sinusoidal positional embeddings and exploiting visual-semantic interactions to model long-range dependencies. We train on a partition of the NASA's Landsat satellite imagery dataset for the United States, containing RGB images at irregular intervals over the past decade, and evaluate on the task of future satellite image forecasting, using metrics such as Content Based Image Retrieval (CBIR) and Intersection over Union (IoU) between the generated and actual future images.
CONTROLS: We compare against a monolithic transformer model with a learned positional embedding function and a baseline diffusion-based image generator conditioned on a text description of the historical sequence.
COST: 720000
PREDICTION: We expect significant improvements over the baseline due to the exploited multimodal interactions and capacity to model long-term dependencies, with potential for temporally consistent forecasts, although difficulties may arise from the long-term gap between training and evaluation points.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Temporal Change Description via Multimodal Large Language Models
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune the multimodal transformer architecture from proposal 1 to perform the task of temporal change description, adapting it to generate natural-language captions that summarize key dynamic changes in satellite image time series. We condition the model on both the sequence of images and their corresponding timestamps, using a custom dataset of annotated satellite image sequences from the National Agriculture Imaging Program (NAIP) that highlights changes in agricultural land use. We evaluate using metrics such as BLEU score and ROUGE for the generated captions, comparing against a baseline MLLM without temporal conditioning and a state-of-the-art video captioning model.
CONTROLS: We study the impact of temporal conditioning, image-text alignment, and multimodal interactions on the performance of the model, as well as its ability to capture causal narratives of change.
COST: 1080000
PREDICTION: We anticipate improvements in temporal change description, leveraging the model's capacity to reason about long-term dependencies and interactions between visual and textual representations, although linguistic complexities and nuance of change might still be challenging to capture accurately.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Exploring Temporal Change Description via Multimodal Large Language Models
PROPOSAL: We refine the previous proposal by incorporating an intermediate language modeling task to fine-tune the model's linguistic capabilities and facilitate the capture of causal narratives. Before generating the final caption, we fine-tune the model on a temporal language modeling task where it predicts the next timestamp or descriptive phrase in the sequence, leveraging the supervised signal to strengthen its ability to reason about temporal relationships and changes. We then evaluate the model's performance on the original captioning task and compare it against the revised baseline.
CONTROLS: We study the impact of the intermediate language modeling task on the model's performance, as well as its ability to generalize to novel temporal relationships and changes.
COST: 1294000
PREDICTION: We expect further improvements in temporal change description, as the model becomes more proficient in capturing causal narratives and interpreting temporal relationships, although additional complexities in the task might lead to diminishing returns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dual-Task Learning for Enhancing Long-term Temporal Understanding
PROPOSAL: We introduce a dual-task learning framework, where the model is trained simultaneously on the tasks of temporal change description and future satellite image forecasting (proposal 1). This setup allows the model to leverage the supervision from both tasks to improve its understanding of long-term temporal relationships and changes. We share the multimodal transformer architecture and embedding spaces across both tasks, but use two separate output heads and task-specific loss functions. We evaluate the model's performance on both tasks and compare it against separate task-trained models.
CONTROLS: We study the impact of task weighting, regularization, and data augmentation on the model's performance, as well as its ability to adapt to novel tasks and temporal relationships.
COST: 2016000
PREDICTION: We expect significant improvements in both tasks, as the model becomes adept at capturing complex long-term temporal relationships and changes through the dual supervision, with potential for temporally consistent forecasts and accurate captions. Challenges may arise from the delicate balance between task-specific and shared representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Temporal Consistency in Satellite Image Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of metrics and a human evaluation protocol to rigorously assess the temporal consistency of forecasted satellite images. The metrics include: (1) temporal coherence, measuring the consistency of changes between consecutive forecasts; (2) trend alignment, evaluating how well the forecast aligns with the historical trend; and (3) novelty, assessing the diversity of forecasted changes relative to previous ones. We also conduct human evaluations to validate the effectiveness of these metrics and gather insights into the types of inconsistencies that models tend to introduce.
CONTROLS: We study the relationship between these metrics and common image quality metrics, such as PSNR and SSIM.
COST: 1036800
PREDICTION: We expect to identify a set of useful metrics for evaluating temporal consistency, although challenges may arise from the lack of ground truth data and the complexity of human perceptions of temporal consistency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Change Captioning via Temporal Clustering and Retrospective Summarization
PROPOSAL: We propose an unsupervised method for change captioning that leverages temporal clustering and retrospective summarization to discover and describe key changes in satellite image time series. We first apply k-means clustering to the sequence of images based on their embeddings, identifying clusters of images that exhibit similar changes. We then generate a caption for each cluster via retrospective summarization, using the images within the cluster to infer the key changes and descriptive phrases. We evaluate the performance of our method on the same dataset as proposal 2 and compare it to the state-of-the-art in unsupervised change captioning.
CONTROLS: We study the impact of clustering parameters and summarization strategies on the quality of generated captions.
COST: 1665600
PREDICTION: We expect to generate captions that are effective at summarizing key changes in thesatellite image time series, although the lack of supervision and ground truth data may limit the accuracy of generated descriptions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Conditional Satellite Image Forecasting via Latent Space Manipulation
PROPOSAL: We propose a method for conditional satellite image forecasting that manipulates the latent space of the multimodal transformer to impose a specific trajectory of changes onto the forecasted image. We use a contrastive loss function to push the forecasted image towards a target class or style, while keeping the overall consistency with the historical sequence. We evaluate the performance of our method on the same dataset as proposal 1 and compare it to state-of-the-art methods in conditional image forecasting.
CONTROLS: We study the impact of contrastive loss weights, latent space initialization, and conditioning schemes on the quality of generated forecasts.
COST: 2496000
PREDICTION: We expect to generate forecasts that are temporally consistent and closely aligned with the target changes, although challenges may arise from the difficulty of imposing specific changes while maintaining overall consistency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fault-Tolerant Forecasts via Model-Based Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose a method for estimating uncertainty in satellite image forecasts, using a probabilistic version of the multimodal transformer. We model the uncertainty as a mixture of Gaussians over the parameter space, and use a variational approximation to approximate the posterior distribution over the parameters. We evaluate the performance of our method on the same dataset as proposal 1 and compare it to state-of-the-art methods in uncertainty estimation.
CONTROLS: We study the impact of variational approximation techniques, uncertainty weighting schemes, and model architectures on the quality of estimated uncertainty.
COST: 3050000
PREDICTION: We expect to generate forecasts with accurate uncertainty estimates, although challenges may arise from the difficulty of modeling complex uncertainty distributions over the parameter space.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Semi-Supervised Learning for Temporal Change Description via Adversarial Training
PROPOSAL: We propose a semi-supervised learning method for temporal change description that leverages adversarial training to encourage the model to generate informative captions even in the absence of labeled data. We train a discriminator to distinguish between captions generated from labeled and unlabeled data, and use this information to adjust the generator's parameters. We evaluate the performance of our method on a dataset with partially labeled captions and compare it to state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods.
CONTROLS: We study the impact of adversarial loss weights, discriminator architectures, and unlabeled data augmentation techniques on the quality of generated captions.
COST: 3400000
PREDICTION: We expect to generate informative captions with good quality, especially in regions with limited labeled data, although challenges may arise from the difficulty of balancing the generator's and discriminator's performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Deployment and Benchmarking of Satellite Change Captioning and Forecasting Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a large-scale deployment of our models on a variety of satellite image time series datasets, including datasets from NASA, ESA, and commercial satellite providers. We benchmark our models on a set of common metrics, including forecasting accuracy, captioning quality, and temporal consistency. We also conduct user studies to evaluate the effectiveness of our models in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: We study the impact of dataset size, model complexity, and deployment settings on the performance of our models.
COST: 43000000
PREDICTION: We expect to be able to deploy our models at scale, with good performance on a variety of satellite image time series datasets, although challenges may arise from the difficulty of dealing with the diversity of datasets and deployment settings.

TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Updating Ensemble Weights in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Assess the effectiveness of updating ensemble weights versus freezing them in an online gradient descent setup on three real-world forecasting benchmarks: traffic flow from INTEL lab's Traffic Prediction dataset, electricity consumption from the M4 competition dataset, and weather forecasting from the public pound Sterling to US Dollar exchange rate historical quotes, using a fixed architecture and varying the ensemble size. 
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline that randomizes ensemble weights and updates all model parameters. 
COST: 900
PREDICTION: We expect updating ensemble weights to outperform the baseline for larger ensemble sizes, but may observe decreased performance if the dataset has strong temporal dependencies, where adapting the entire architecture is more effective than adjusting ensemble weights.

TITLE: Investigating the Effectiveness of Adaptation Module Architecture in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of different adapter module architectures (e.g., simple multilayer perceptrons, linear layers, and residual connections) on adapting a pre-trained LSTM model for online time series forecasting on two datasets: US electricity consumption from the M4 competition dataset and a subset of theanon therm database for wind power production. 
CONTROLS: Ablate the adapter component entirely and compare to the baseline of updating the entire model architecture. 
COST: 1650
PREDICTION: We expect that residual connections will outperform the other adapter architectures, as they allow for more expressive updates while maintaining stability, but may also observe that the most straightforward adapter design (simple multilayer perceptrons) performs well in early time steps before the more complex adapters' advantage becomes apparent.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Assessing the Benefits and Drawbacks of Partial Model Updates in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Systematically study the impact of partial model updates (i.e., updating only the final prediction layer or a specific set of layers) for online time series forecasting using a pre-trained deep forecasting model, evaluated on the INTEL lab's Traffic Prediction dataset, the M4 competition dataset for electricity consumption and a standard weather forecasting dataset (no further details yet). 
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline that updates the entire model and an ablation where no model parameters are updated. Investigate sensitivity to hyperparameters such as learning rate and the specific set of layers being updated. 
COST: 2250
PREDICTION: We anticipate benefits from partial updates in terms of reduced computational overhead and numerical stability, but may also note a trade-off with model expressiveness and robustness to concept drift.

ACTION: REVISE 3 
TITLE: Assessing the Benefits and Drawbacks of Partial Model Updates in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Extend the previous proposal by incorporating an additional set of experiments that specifically examine the impact of partial model updates in multi-step forecasting scenarios. Investigate how different partial update strategies, such as freezing all layers except the final prediction layer, or updating the recurrence and dense layers separately, perform under delayed and noisy feedback, and for more future steps, again on the INTEL lab's Traffic Prediction dataset, the M4 competition dataset for electricity consumption and a standard weather forecasting dataset. 
CONTROLS: Retain the baseline and ablation controls from the original proposal, and continue to investigate sensitivity to learning rate and the specific set of layers being updated. Evaluate the effectiveness of different regularization techniques (e.g., weight decay, early stopping) for preventing overfitting in partial update scenarios. 
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: We expect that in multi-step forecasting scenarios, partial updates can struggle to adapt to changes in more far-off steps, leading to biased forecasts and larger errors; still, the right partial update strategy could help to maintain performance and provide faster adaptation to near-term changes; merits of specific design choices should become clear.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Normalization Techniques in Addressing Distribution Shift in Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Explore the effectiveness of different normalization methods (e.g., batch normalization, layer normalization, instance normalization) in addressing distribution shift in online time series forecasting when using a pre-trained deep forecasting model. Assess their performance on an online adaptation scenario, varying the task and dataset and targeted at traffic flow forecasting, using a subset of SYNCHRON data, and weather forecasting using the ME@1 evaluation metrics.

TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Online Gradient Descent with Unbiased Gradient Estimates
PROPOSAL: Provide a theoretical analysis of the convergence rate of online gradient descent when unbiased gradient estimates are used, especially in the context of time series forecasting. Derive bounds on the regret of the algorithm, and investigate how the properties of the time series data (e.g., stationarity, ergodicity) affect the performance of the algorithm. Provide a thorough comparison with the existing analysis of online gradient descent with biased gradient estimates, highlighting the benefits and limitations of using unbiased estimates.

TITLE: Empirical Investigation of Multi-Task Learning for Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of multi-task learning for online time series forecasting, where a single model is trained to predict multiple related time series simultaneously. Evaluate the performance of multi-task models on a range of online time series forecasting benchmarks, including traffic flow, weather forecasting, and electricity consumption, and compare it to the performance of single-task models and models that use task-incremental learning. 
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline that trains a separate model for each task using a standard online gradient descent algorithm, and evaluate the performance of different multi-task learning architectures, such as shared weights and hard parameter sharing. 
COST: 12000

TITLE: A Modular Framework for Online Time Series Forecasting Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Develop a modular framework for online time series forecasting adaptation that allows researchers and practitioners to easily compare and combine different adaptation methods. The framework will include a set of core modules that provide common functionality, such as data preprocessing and model selection, as well as a set of interchangeable adaptation modules that provide different adaptation strategies. Evaluate the performance of the framework on a range of online time series forecasting benchmarks, using different combinations of adaptation modules. 
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline that uses a traditional online gradient descent algorithm without adaptation, and evaluate the performance of different adaptation modules, such as normalization, partial model updates, and multi-task learning.

PREDICTION: We expect that the modular framework will provide a powerful tool for researchers and practitioners to investigate and compare different adaptation methods for online time series forecasting, leading to improved performance and greater flexibility in adaptive forecasting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Hybrid Retrieval with Text and Image Encoders
PROPOSAL: We will test the effectiveness of combining a state-of-the-art ColPali-based late-interaction multimodal retriever with a lightweight dense text retriever, specifically the AnsiBERT model, on the depuis dataset, which is a public benchmark for visual document retrieval. We will train the ColPali-based model and Ansibert model separately, then evaluate their performance in a hybrid setting by aggregating their similarity scores at query time. Additionally, we will compare the performance of the hybrid model with a strong vision-centric baseline, the ColBERT model, to gauge the effectiveness of text-image hybrid retrieval.
CONTROLS: (1) ColBERT without hybridization, (2) Ansibert without hybridization, (3) a ColPali baseline with reduced capacity, ablated to match the computational complexity of the Ansibert model.
COST: 12300
PREDICTION: We expect the hybrid model to outperform both individual models, with the ColPali-based model contributing more significantly to the final ranking, and the Ansibert model providing a modest boost to the top-N accuracy. The combination may struggle to integrate effectively, leading to performance drops in certain retrieval scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Architecture-Agnostic Aggregation
PROPOSAL: To create a lightweight and practical aggregation scheme for combining the similarity scores of two heterogeneous retrievers, we will explore applying a learnable compression layer to map the high-dimensional similarity scores into a lower-dimensional shared space, where they can be efficiently compared. This compression layer will be trained jointly with the ColPali-based and Ansibert models to optimize performance of the hybrid system. We will compare this approach with a baseline aggregation method that takes the maximum or average of the two similarity scores.
CONTROLS: (1) baseline max aggregation, (2) baseline average aggregation, (3) no aggregation (simply summing the scores without mapping to a shared space).
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: The proposed learnable compression layer will significantly improve the performance of the hybrid system, allowing it to effectively integrate the strengths of both models. The maximum aggregation baseline may struggle with diminishing returns for highly correlated scores. Average aggregation could help to reduce the noise in highly variable scores, but it may lose important distinctions between similar, yet distinct, documents.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Online Latency and Index Memory Trade-Off
PROPOSAL: We will systematically vary the capacity of the ColPali-based model and the Ansibert model, training new pairs of models with reduced capacities (e.g., fewer parameters) while maintaining their individual performance. We will then evaluate the online latency and index memory usage of the hybrid system for each pair of models, measuring the impact of capacity reduction on these critical performance metrics. This will help us understand the trade-off between model capacity and efficiency in the hybrid system.
CONTROLS: (1) maintaining the original capacity of models, (2) reducing capacity while degrading individual performance.
COST: 18900
PREDICTION: By reducing the capacity of the stronger ColPali-based model, we can significantly decrease the online latency and index memory usage of the hybrid system without compromising its performance. However, reducing the capacity of the weaker Ansibert model may have a limited impact on the overall trade-off due to its relative weakness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Domain Adaptation and Robustness
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the performance of the hybrid system on different domains from the depuis dataset, such as scientific articles, product manuals, and financial reports, to assess its ability to generalize across domains. We will also evaluate its robustness to common challenges like on/padding, camera angles, and font variations. To further stress-test its abilities, we will artificially introduce noise into the image features of the ColPali-based model and analyze the system's capacity to filter out this noise and maintain retrieval accuracy.
CONTROLS: (1) original test setup without domain adaptation or robustness evaluation, (2) random forest domain adaptation baseline.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: The hybrid system will exhibit strong performance on most domains, with a slight decline in performance on the product manuals domain, which tends to have more variable layout and formatting. However, its performance may degrade significantly when faced with artificially introduced noise in the image features. The ColPali-based model's reliance on vision-language understanding may hinder its capacity to filter out this noise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Feature Saliency and Interpretability
PROPOSAL: We will use feature saliency methods, such as Integrated Gradients, to analyze the feature importance of the hybrid system and identify which aspects of the text and image features contribute most to the retrieval accuracy. We will visualize the attention weights learned by the aggregation layer to gain insights into how the system combines the text and image features. This analysis will help us understand the decision-making process of the hybrid system and identify potential areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: (1) attention visualization for individual models without hybridization, (2) feature importance analysis for the baseline max and average aggregation methods.
COST: 38800
PREDICTION: The feature saliency analysis will reveal that the hybrid system relies more heavily on the image features, particularly those related to layout and formatting, which are crucial for document retrieval. The attention visualization will show that the aggregation layer tends to focus on the most informative text features, while down-weighting less relevant image features.

LIME will allow us to generate synthetic data that imitates the behavior of the hybrid system, enabling us to identify the most important features and interactions between text and image features. This will provide a more nuanced understanding of the system's strengths and weaknesses.
